notes.text: Acts xxii, 3, &c.; Acts xxvi, 9, &c.
Bound — By the connivance, if not authority, of the governor, under Aretas the king. See Acts ix, 14, 24.

And suddenly — When God suddenly and vehemently attacks a sinner, it is the highest act of mercy. So Saul, when his rage was come to the height, is taught not to breathe slaughter. And what was wanting in time to confirm him in his discipleship, is compensated by the inexpressible terror he sustained. By his also the suddenly constituted apostle was guarded against the grand snare into which novices are apt to fall.
He heard a voice — Severe, yet full of grace.
To kick against the goads — is a Syriac proverb, expressing an attempt that brings nothing but pain.
It shall be told thee — So God himself sends Saul to be taught by a man, as the angel does Cornelius, chap. x, 5. Admirable condescension! that the Lord deals with us by men, like ourselves.

glossa.text: *And Saul.* He returns to that which he had said above: *Saul was still laying waste the Church. Of threatenings,* etc. Terrifying with threats, he afflicted with slaughter those present: it is doubted whether he killed or scourged, or did both. *Breathing.* He breathes after the manner of fire, and not incited by another he himself set others on fire.

*And falling.* Terrified, he flees back to the ground, or as one adoring he falls upon his face.

*Why me,* etc. ((BEDA.)) He says not: Why dost thou persecute, etc., *as far as, As long as you did it to one of these least ones, you did it to me ((Matth. XXV))*.
*I am Jesus.* He calls himself not God nor the Son of God, but, Receive, he says, the weak things of my humility, and lay aside the scales of thy pride.

notes.text: Cometh — Speedily and in due season.
Mountain — My kingdom: kingdoms are usually called mountains in prophetical writings.
Profit — What wilt thou gain by it? The dust - Shall they that are dead celebrate thy goodness in the land of the living? Or, shall my dust praise thee?

Sackcloth — Given me occasion to put off that sackcloth, which they used to wear in times of mourning, Esth iv, 1 chap. xxxv, 13 Isaiah xxxii, 11 Joel i, 13. Girded - With joy, as with a garment, surrounding me on every side.

My glory — My tongue. David professes his confidence in God, intermixing prayer to him, ver. 1-8. Complains to God and prays for deliverance, ver. 9-18. Concludes with giving glory to God, and encouraging others to trust him, ver. 19-24. To the chief musician, A psalm of David.

glossa.text: *O Lord my God, I have cried to thee,* etc. ((AUG.)) Christ, etc., *as far as* but not in the dedication.
*Into the pit.* ((HIER.)) That is, out of the pit of hell, where the souls of sinners are, lest, like them, I should fall headlong into death.
*Confess ye,* etc. ((AUG.)) Because out of his own goodness and holiness, not ours, he was mindful of us.

*For wrath.* ((ID.)) That is, vengeance, by which he avenged upon us the first sin, which by death you have loosed.

*At evening.* ((ID.)) Because wrath, etc., *as far as* that is, in the time of grace after the time before the law and under the law.

((HIER.)) *At evening.* Because, when the Lord had suffered and been buried, the Apostles and the women continued in weeping and groaning. *And in the morning gladness.* Because coming to the sepulchre in the morning they received from the Angels the glory of the resurrection. *Weeping.* ((CASS.)) It shall abide for men who look toward the evening, at which Adam turned aside and went out from paradise: but there shall be gladness for those who look toward the morning, at which Christ rose again.

*But I.* How he acted before the dedication and deserved it. ((AUG., CASS.)) He acts at evening. But I, while abundance was mine in paradise, said: I shall not be moved from this good, believing the devil who said: *Thou shalt not die the death ((Gen. III))* . But, O Lord, in *thy will thou hast given strength to my beauty;* which is, I was good and strong not of myself, but of thee. And that thou mightest show it: *Thou hast turned away thy face,* that is, thou hast sent me forth out of paradise: but now, set here, *I will cry to thee,* etc.

*Thou hast turned away.* ((CASS.)) God turned away his face from Christ, by exposing him to the passion and to death; and thus Christ was troubled: *My soul is sorrowful even unto death. ((Matth. XVI.)) Troubled.* ((AUG.)) Calling to mind that time of trouble and of misery, and set in it, I hear the voice of the head who is to die for me, saying: *To thee, O Lord, will I cry.*

*What profit is there in my blood.* ((ID.)) He shows the necessity by which he does not suffer him to go down into corruption. *Whilst I go down into corruption.* For if I do not rise again at once, and the body is corrupted, I shall announce to no one, I shall gain no one. Confession is twofold, let us never be without it: when it is ill with us in tribulations, let us confess our sins; when it is well, let us confess praise to God in the exultation of justice.
*The Lord hath heard.* ((CASS.)) He treats of how he received it, namely the dedication. He said: I will cry, I will beseech, but the Lord heard me beseeching.

*Thou hast cut my sackcloth.* ((ID.)) Sackcloth is a rough garment, granted for the use of labour or in a time of sadness, as to the Ninivites; that is, human flesh, which was rent by dying: and there came forth the corn of the glorious resurrection, or of the godhead. Or else, the penalty of sin, which being destroyed in the resurrection, the godhead before hidden was brought forth: just as what the sack conceals whole, it opens when rent. ((AUG.)) Sackcloth of goats or of kids is mortality, which Christ drew or took from sinners; whence: *Whilst they were troublesome to me, I was clothed with haircloth ((Psal. XXXIV))*, that they might not see what was within.
*I shall not be pricked.* ((ID.)) I shall not now die unto the end. *O Lord God, I will confess to thee for ever.* What is: *I will confess to thee for ever?* For ever I will praise thee.

notes.text: And I saw — The many angels. And heard - The voice and the number of them. Round about the elders - So forming the third circle. It is remarkable, that men are represented through this whole vision as nearer to God than any of the angels. And the number of them was - At least two hundred millions, and two millions over. And yet these were but a part of the holy angels. Afterward, chap. vii, 11, St. John heard them all.

Worthy is the Lamb — The elders said, ver. 9, "Worthy art thou." They were more nearly allied to him than the angels. To receive the power, &c. - This sevenfold applause answers the seven seals, of which the four former describe all visible, the latter all invisible, things, made subject to the Lamb. And every one of these seven words bears a resemblance to the seal which it answers.

And every creature — In the whole universe, good or bad. In the heaven, on the earth, under the earth, on the sea - With these four regions of the world, agrees the fourfold word of praise. What is in heaven, says blessing; what is on earth, honour; what is under the earth, glory: what is on the sea, strength; is unto him. This praise from all creatures begins before the opening of the first seal; but it continues from that time to eternity, according to the capacity of each. His enemies must acknowledge his glory; but those in heaven say, Blessed be God and the Lamb. This royal manifesto is, as it were, a proclamation, showing how Christ fulfils all things, and "every knee bows to him," not only on earth, but also in heaven, and under the earth. This book exhausts all things, 1 Cor. xv, 27, 28, and is suitable to an heart enlarged as the sand of the sea. It inspires the attentive and intelligent reader with such a magnanimity, that he accounts nothing in this world great; no, not the whole frame of visible nature, compared to the immense greatness of what he is here called to behold, yea, and in part, to inherit. St. John has in view, through the whole following vision, what he has been now describing, namely, the four living creatures, the elders, the angels, and all creatures, looking together at the opening of the seven seals. The seven seals are not distinguished from each other by specifying the time of them. They swiftly follow the letters to the seven churches, and all begin almost at the same time. By the four former is shown, that all the public occurrences of all ages and nations, as empire, war, provision, calamities, are made subject to Christ. And instances are intimated of the first in the east, the second in the west, the third in the south, the fourth in the north and the whole world. The contents, as of the phials and trumpets, so of the seals, are shown by the songs of praise and thanksgiving annexed to them. They contain therefore "the power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing," which the Lamb received. The four former have a peculiar connection with each other; and so have the three latter seals. The former relate to visible things, toward the four quarters to which the four living creatures look. Before we proceed, it may be observed,

glossa.text:
*I saw.* Not only the living creatures and the elders bearing the same witness out of their office, but also *I heard,*

 *The voice of angels.* That is, of the supernal spirits who fortify and guard the Church, who rejoice over the restored fellowship of the saints, who bear witness to Christ, and who both at his nativity, when they appeared to the shepherds, and at his passion, and at his resurrection and ascension, testified that the judge would come. Or the angels are the lesser subjects in the Church, leading an angelic life, who surround and honour their preachers and their judges, consenting to their testimony and conforming themselves to it. *Of many round about the throne and of the living creatures and of the elders,* etc. The more they are, the greater the attestation, and the greater the joy. *Thousands of thousands.* He set down this number, because that is finite with God which to men is infinite.
*Wisdom, and strength,* etc. The knowledge of all things, even as the Word united to himself has it.

*Benediction.* That is, the increase which we have in good works, *and honour* which follows therefrom, *and glory* from the virtues which we receive in baptism, *and power* by which we resist concupiscences, let it be attributed not to us, but to thee.

*And the four living creatures.* All the elders and the living creatures give their assent to the testimony of the angels. *They fell upon their faces,* etc. They are not proud because they judge others, but they humble themselves.

notes.text: There were together — At home, in one house.
They knew not that it was Jesus — Probably their eyes were holden.

They were not able to draw it for the multitude of fishes — This was not only a demonstration of the power of our Lord, but a kind supply for them and their families, and such as might be of service to them, when they waited afterward in Jerusalem. It was likewise an emblem of the great success which should attend them as fishers of men.

Peter girt on his upper coat (for he was stript of it before) — Reverencing the presence of his Lord: and threw himself into the sea - To swim to him immediately. The love of Christ draws men through fire and water.
Come ye and dine — Our Lord needed not food. And none presumed - To ask a needless question.
The third time — That he appeared to so many of the apostles together.

Simon, son of Jonah — The appellation Christ had given him, when be made that glorious confession, Matt. xvi, 16, the remembrance of which might make him more deeply sensible of his late denial of him whom he had so confessed. Lovest thou me? - Thrice our Lord asks him, who had denied him thrice: more than these - Thy fellow disciples do? - Peter thought so once, Matt. xxvi, 33, but he now answers only- I love thee, without adding more than these. Thou knowest - He had now learnt by sad experience that Jesus knew his heart. My lambs - The weakest and tenderest of the flock.
Because he said the third time — As if he did not believe him.

When thou art old — He lived about thirty-six years after this: another shall gird thee - They were tied to the cross till the nails were driven in; and shall carry thee - With the cross: whither thou wouldest not - According to nature; to the place where the cross was set up.
By what death he should glorify God — It is not only by acting, but chiefly by suffering, that the saints glorify God. Follow me - Showing hereby likewise what death he should die.

glossa.text: *Afterwards he manifested.* Having left all things they had followed Jesus. But if after the death of Jesus, before he was restored to them alive, they had taken up their former craft again, they might seem to have done this out of despair; but after he was restored alive, after they had received the spirit of his breathing, after his words: *As the Father hath sent me, I also send you,* suddenly they become what they had been, fishers, not of men but of fishes. But it is to be known that they were not forbidden to seek their living by their own lawful craft, the integrity of the apostolate being preserved, since they had not whereof to live; and so, as they laboured, God added the necessary things which he had promised; but here their want was disposed, that in the fishing such great sacraments might be displayed.

*This now.* Not that he was manifested only three times, but he refers it to the days: on the first day, on which he rose again; after eight days; on this day, when he did this concerning the fishes. The manifestations therefore are numbered according to the days. The first, however often it was made, on the one day of the resurrection. The second, after eight days; and this is the third. In this third manifestation this Gospel is ended.

*When therefore they had dined.* Jesus knows what he asks, whether he loves more; Peter says what he knows of himself, that is, that he loves. And because he does not know concerning the others how much they love, therefore he is silent as to whether he loves more than they. Behold, he teaches not to determine rashly about hidden things; and by the earlier peril of his denial he answers of himself more cautiously.

*Feed my lambs.* If thou love me, *feed my lambs.* Not as thine own: seek my glory in them, not thine own; my gains, not thine, because the love of God is proved in the love of the neighbour. But he who denies the work of piety to his neighbours loves God less. And this charity is given out of divine grace. Which John silently hints at when, asking about love, he says here what he does not say elsewhere: *Simon, son of John,* that is, obedient by the grace of God, because that he loves and obeys more ardently than the rest is nothing save the grace of God.

*He saith to him the third time.* He asks what he knew, not once, but again and a third time; and a third time he hears from Peter that he is loved, and a third time he bids him feed the sheep. To the threefold denial a threefold confession is rendered, lest the tongue serve love less than fear. And as it was the judgment of fear to deny the shepherd, so it is the office of love to feed the Lord's flock. *Peter was grieved. ((AUG.))* Even when his sins are forgiven a man endures the misery into which nevertheless he came out of sin. For the punishment is drawn out longer than the fault, and the fault would seem no small thing if the punishment were taken away along with it. It is therefore either for the showing of the misery that is owed, or for the amending of a slipping life, or for the exercise of necessary patience, that punishment holds a man for a time, even him whom guilt no longer holds as guilty; and this is the condition of these days, to be wept over, but not to be blamed. *Feed.* To feed the sheep is to comfort believers lest they fail, to provide earthly supports, if it be necessary, for those subject to one, to offer examples of the virtues, to withstand adversaries, to correct those who sin.

*But when thou shalt be old.* He foretells that he will suffer, who had foretold that he would deny; strengthened by the resurrection he could now do that which, while weak, he promised before its time. Now he does not fear the ending of this life, because, the Lord rising again, the example of another life went before.

*And when he had said this.* These things being said, Jesus began to go away; and, not yet understanding what he had heard, *Follow me,* Peter began to follow with the going of his feet; and John also followed, who knew that he was loved.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Christ is risen!
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
They fished all night and caught nothing,
and at daybreak a voice from the shore filled the nets.
You turned our mourning into dancing;
by the charcoal fire he asked, Do you love me? Then feed my sheep.
Come and have breakfast, the risen Lord says.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Stand on the shore in the gray of early morning, your nets empty, your arms tired from a long and fruitless night.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
A figure on the beach calls out, cast the net again — and it comes up so full it will not break.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
There is a charcoal fire going, and fish on it, and bread, and the smell of breakfast drifts across the water: Come and eat.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
By that same fire he asks the question three times over: Do you love me? Then feed my sheep.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
You turned our weeping into dancing; we come to the fire to be fed and sent:
Christ is risen, Alleluia!

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: The nets are empty, the long night gone.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
A voice from the shore fills them to breaking.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Bread and fish on the fire: Come and have breakfast.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
Do you love me? Feed my sheep. Come, let us worship.
Christ is risen, Alleluia!
